sens: one who marries the daughter of a family
one who becomes a member of the family through marriage
to form a family alliance through marriage
H2859B.detail:
1. The son-in-law is the man who marries a daughter: he is the husband from the perspective of his in-laws. The Hebrew word primarily evokes this kinship relationship created by marriage. David becomes the "son-in-law of the king" by marrying Saul's daughter (1 Samuel 18:21-26): it is a promise of alliance between two families.
2. The word also designates the alliance itself, the act of "becoming a son-in-law," that is, entering into marriage with a daughter from another family. This is why one can speak of "contracting" or "forming" alliances through marriage (Deuteronomy 7:3; Joshua 23:12): it is not only a personal union, but a fusion of two households.
3. In a broader sense, it means establishing family relationships, or more strongly: bringing one family into another. When the Law forbids Israel to "intermarry" with neighboring peoples (Deuteronomy 7:3), the risk is not only personal but collective: it is the identity of Israel that would be diluted in the idolatry of the nations.
H2859B.origine: The Hebrew word חָתַן (chatan) comes from a root that expresses the idea of uniting, binding. The form we read here is an infinitive; in the texts, the participle is encountered ("one who is a son-in-law") to designate a man married to a daughter of the family. The word also appears as a noun: "the son-in-law" designates the married man, and "the bride" his wife. This root common to Semitic languages refers to a fundamental reality: marriage is a bond, an alliance between families.
H2859B.emploi: This verb appears eleven times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical narratives and the Law. It first describes the concrete action of becoming a son-in-law (David with Saul, 1 Samuel 18). But it also expresses a political strategy: kings marry to forge alliances with other powers (1 Kings 3:1; 2 Chronicles 18:1). The Law of Israel uses this word to prohibit marital alliances with idolatrous peoples (Deuteronomy 7:3; Joshua 23:12): here, marriage is not a simple private act, but a spiritual danger for the people. It is finally the term used by Ezra to denounce mixed marriages that occurred in exile (Ezra 9:14).
H2859B.portee: This word reminds the reader that marriage, in the Bible, is never just a personal matter: it is an alliance that unites two families, even two peoples. For Israel, it raises a serious question: with whom can one ally without losing one's identity and faithfulness to God? The divine refusal of mixed marriages is not contempt, but protection: to remain a people set apart for God. This question remains relevant for the Christian seeking to live out their faith in a world that does not share it.

sens: one who has married the daughter of another family, bound by marriage to his father-in-law
the young man at the time of his engagement or marriage
one who enters into a family alliance through marriage
H2860.detail:
1. The primary meaning is concrete and social: it is the man who has married a daughter and thus becomes a member of the family of her father. In Lot's case, he is asked to bring out his "sons-in-law" — the husbands of his daughters (Genesis 19:12). It is an established and recognized family bond that creates mutual obligations: Saul calls David his "son-in-law" after his marriage to Michal (1 Samuel 18:18).
2. The word also designates the fiancé at the time of engagement or marriage, in the joy of the wedding. In Isaiah 61:10, the fiancé adorns himself with a diadem, a symbol of his dignity and joy on that day: it is the image of the young groom radiating in the presence of his beloved.
3. By extension, the term evokes the alliance that marriage seals: one who enters into a new family through the bonds of marriage, assuming the alliances, responsibilities, and rights that follow.
H2860.origine: The Hebrew word חָתָן likely comes from a root meaning "to bind" or "to unite," as marriage is primarily a union that binds two families together. In the Old Testament, it is often used alongside "kallah" (bride) to describe the new or forming couple. The context of marriage, where two families unite, is at the heart of the image.
H2860.emploi: The word appears 19 times in the Old Testament, mainly in narrative prose and poetry. It first describes concrete family relationships: Lot has sons-in-law (Genesis 19:12), David becomes the son-in-law of the king (1 Samuel 18:18), Nehemiah has sons-in-law among the leaders of Judah (Nehemiah 6:18). It also qualifies the fiancé at the time of marriage or celebration, in a joyful context: the fiancé adorns himself in Isaiah 61:10, and the songs of the fiancé resound on festive days (Jeremiah 16:9). The word takes on a tone of nostalgia or mourning when the prophetic threat demands that these songs cease: no more voice of fiancé or fiancée means the end of marital joy and the renewal of the community.
H2860.portee: This word reminds us that marriage is an alliance that binds not only two individuals but two families, with responsibilities and blessings. The joy of the fiancé in the prophetic texts illustrates how a happy and fruitful marriage was at the heart of Israel's hope. Its absence in the prophetic threat shows that divine judgment reaches to the very sources of family and community life. For the Christian reader, the image of the fiancé and fiancée in rejoicing also offers a figure of the union between Christ and the Church.

sens: Ceremony and festivities of marriage
Solemn union of two people before witnesses
Day of rejoicing and celebration
H2861.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the marriage ceremony and the festivities that accompany it — not only the exchange of consent but the entire joyful and public event. In Song of Solomon 3:11, it is the "day of his engagement" when King Solomon wears the crown that his mother placed on him: it is a solemn moment, imbued with royal dignity.
2. More broadly, the word evokes the official and recognized union of two beings, sealed before the community. It is a contract and an alliance, not just a private feeling.
3. Through its context in the Song, the word emphasizes joy: "the day of the joy of his heart." Engagements are a moment of gladness, celebration, where beauty and happiness are highlighted.
H2861.origine: The Hebrew word חֲתֻנָּה (cha­tun­nah) comes from the root חתן (cha­tan), which designates the son-in-law or one who enters into the marriage alliance. The underlying image is that of entry, of a union contracted. The word is formed as an abstract feminine noun, emphasizing the event and the institution rather than the individuals.
H2861.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Song of Solomon 3:11. It designates the day of King Solomon's engagement, a moment when he wears the crown and joy reigns. Although rare, this word expresses the idea that marriage is a public, solemn, and joyful event, worthy of the highest persons. In the context of the Song, a poetic celebration of love, engagements embody the fullness and beauty of union.
H2861.portee: The word reminds readers that marriage, in the Bible, is a public and happy event, an alliance worthy of respect and joy. This unique usage in the Song shows that the love between a man and a woman deserves royal dignity and communal celebration. It is a call to see marriage not merely as a private affair, but as a gift from God that fills the heart with joy and is part of the life of the entire community.

sens: Seize and take forcefully, by tearing or abruptly
Snatch, steal, take away suddenly and irresistibly
H2862.detail:
1. The verb "remove" expresses the action of taking something forcefully and quickly, as if it were being torn from someone's hands. It is a sudden and violent gesture. In Job 9:12, God "removes" (that is, takes away) without anyone being able to oppose it: the image is that of an irresistible power that seizes what it wants.
2. The word also evokes the idea of stealing or snatching: one who "removes" acts like a thief or with tyrannical force. He takes what does not belong to him, or at least what one believed they had rights to. In the context of God in Job 9:12, it is indeed absolute power: God can take back life, prosperity, health without man having a say in the matter.
H2862.origine: The Hebrew verb חָתַף (cataph) comes from a root that fundamentally means "to seize" or "to tear away." It belongs to the family of verbs denoting abrupt and violent action. This root expresses the idea of a sudden taking, without preparation or gentleness. The word always implies a rapid movement and a certain force.
H2862.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Job 9:12. It is part of Job's discourse, recognizing God's sovereign power in the face of human weakness. Job asserts that if God "removes" (holds back, takes back), no one can question Him. It is a rare word, used to emphasize the irresistibility of divine action: one cannot stop God, one cannot question or contradict Him. The context is that of theodicy, the question of evil and God's sovereignty.
H2862.portee: This word reminds the believer that God has absolute authority over all creation and everything that lives. No human force can oppose His will. At the same time, Job humbly recognizes this reality: God can take away what He has given, and man can only submit to His wisdom and justice, even when he does not understand everything.

sens: One who steals and plunders by violence
One who sets traps to steal
H2863.detail:
1. The bandit is a wrongdoer who steals by force and violence, a criminal who robs his victims on the roads or elsewhere. In Proverbs 23:28, the adulterous woman is compared to a bandit who sets traps: she waits for her prey to seduce and ruin them, just like a highway robber waits for his victim to attack.
2. The word emphasizes the predatory and calculated aspect of this act: the bandit does not steal by chance; he prepares his move, he sets traps. He is someone aggressive and treacherous, who intentionally hunts to steal.
H2863.origine: The Hebrew word חֶתֶף (chéteph) comes from a root that means "to seize" or "to tear away." It describes one who takes by force, who snatches, who plunders. This root evokes the image of a predator who pounces on its prey and violently snatches it away. The family of words also includes the concept of loot, of what has been taken by violence.
H2863.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Proverbs 23:28. It is used metaphorically to describe the adulterous woman: just as a bandit sets traps to rob travelers, she sets traps to seduce and ruin men. This comparison emphasizes that adultery is a predatory and deliberate act, intended to destroy its target. The context of the Book of Proverbs shows that this term is used to warn of real and serious moral dangers.
H2863.portee: This image of the bandit reminds us that the sin of adultery is not trivial: it destroys, it robs the one who commits it of their freedom, dignity, and salvation. It is a call to vigilance against the seductions that can cause us to lose our true spiritual riches.

sens: To dig or bore a solid surface, like a wall or a house
To break and enter a dwelling to steal
To row, to move a boat by stirring the water
To penetrate, to sink into a difficult-to-access place
H2864.detail:
1. The primary meaning is a physical act: to dig, to make a hole or an opening in something solid. In Ezekiel 8:8, God commands the prophet: "Pierce the wall!" — it is about breaking through the wall to reach what is hidden behind it. It is a concrete, manual act.

2. This verb also describes breaking and entering, the crime of a burglar who forces his way into a house at night. Job 24:16 speaks of those who "force their way into houses" — it is the same Hebrew verb, applied to the criminal act of piercing the wall to plunder.

3. In a nautical context, "to row" or "to move a boat" involves the same physical act: digging or cutting through the water with the oars to progress. Although this meaning is present in the definition, the provided usages do not clearly illustrate it.

4. Figuratively, the word also describes the ability to penetrate or to sink even into the most inaccessible places. Amos 9:2 shows this: "If they penetrate into the realm of the dead, My hand will take them from there" — God asserts that nothing can escape His grasp, not even the depths of the earth.
H2864.origine: This Hebrew verb primarily denotes the action of digging or boring, stemming from the concrete image of working with wood or stone. It is not a very productive root in biblical Hebrew: the word remains focused on the physical idea of piercing, without many derivatives. It is mostly found in prophetic narratives (Ezekiel), where the image of piercing takes on symbolic significance — crossing an obstacle to discover what is hidden.
H2864.emploi: This verb appears 7 times in the Hebrew Bible. Most occurrences are concentrated in the book of Ezekiel (4 occurrences), where it describes the action of the prophet piercing the wall of the temple to uncover hidden idolatries (8:8) and Ezekiel symbolically enacting the escape of the prince of Judah (12:5, 12:7, 12:12). It is also found in Job 24:16, where it depicts the crime of the burglar, and in Amos 9:2, where it expresses the impossibility of escaping God by sinking anywhere. The verb thus oscillates between the concrete physical meaning (to pierce, to force) and the figurative or symbolic usage (to penetrate the inaccessible).
H2864.portee: This word reminds the reader that nothing escapes God, even what seems well hidden behind walls or deep in the realm of the dead. For the believer, it invites awareness that secret acts are known to God and that His justice reaches everywhere. It is also a word of judgment: the walls that are forced, the obstacles that are pierced, never remain invisible before the Lord.

sens: To experience a paralyzing fear, a sudden fright
To be broken, destroyed, annihilated in strength or will
To tremble, to be seized with terror in the face of an imminent threat
To lose courage, assurance, confidence in the face of danger
H2865.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the state of one who is seized by intense and sudden fear, which paralyzes them. It is the fright that grips you when confronted with the unexpected or terrifying. In Deuteronomy 1:21, Moses encourages Israel: "do not be afraid, and do not be terrified" — one must not let fear overwhelm them even before entering into battle.
2. The word can also express the state of destruction or physical breaking: something that has collapsed, abolished, that no longer exists. Jeremiah 48:39 shows this: "How broken it is!" — Moab is annihilated, collapsed.
3. To tremble and to be afraid go together: it is the visible reaction of the body in the face of terror. In Isaiah 31:9, the leaders "will tremble before the banner" of the Lord.
4. Terror can also mean losing one's assurance, momentum, or ability to act. Job 32:15 shows people who "are afraid" and "no longer respond" — fear has rendered them unable to speak.
H2865.origine: This Hebrew root primarily expresses the idea of breaking, collapsing — something that breaks, that falls apart. From this comes the image of a human being internally broken by fear, emptied of strength and courage. The word appears 46 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the prophets and accounts of war or divine judgment.
H2865.emploi: The verb appears 46 times in biblical Hebrew, mainly in the prophetic books (Jeremiah, Isaiah) and historical accounts (Joshua, Samuel, Chronicles). Often, it describes the fear that grips the enemies of Israel or the people when they doubt God: "do not be afraid and do not be terrified" recurs as a refrain of encouragement (Deuteronomy 1:21; 1 Chronicles 22:13). It can also depict collective terror: the earth itself "is seized with horror" (Jeremiah 14:4). In some cases, it means that something is "broken" or "annihilated" in the literal sense (Jeremiah 48:39). The nuance varies: sometimes it is psychological fear, sometimes it is actual annihilation, but the central idea is that of a broken force.
H2865.portee: This word teaches Christians that fear is the enemy of faith. When God repeats "do not be terrified," He does not deny real dangers, but invites us to place our trust in Him rather than to be paralyzed. Recognizing when one is seized with terror is already a step towards prayer and confident surrender to God.

sens: Intense feeling of fear and trouble in the face of a threat
State of deep affliction and moral distress
H2866.detail:
1. Anguish is a strong and overwhelming fear, a fright that seizes one who feels in danger or abandoned. In Job 6:21, Job speaks of his "anguish" in the presence of his friends: he is going through such a terrible trial that fear and distress overwhelm him, and he hopes to find comfort from them.
2. The word can also describe a broader moral affliction, a state of deep turmoil in the face of life's overwhelming circumstances. It is that fear that grips when one feels alone and misunderstood in their suffering.
H2866.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes trembling and consternation, the idea of something that makes one recoil in fear. The root suggests a reaction of the body and soul in the face of what threatens and terrifies. It is a rare word in biblical Hebrew, painting a violent feeling rather than an ordinary fear.
H2866.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Job 6:21. Job, stripped of everything and covered in sores, laments that his companions, witnesses to his distress, abandon him instead of supporting him. His anguish before the succession of his misfortunes and this solitude finds no consolation. It is a cry from a man who is suffocating under the weight of affliction.
H2866.portee: This word from Job reminds us that anguish is a reality that God knows and recognizes in our lives. It also calls us to compassion: when we see someone in distress and anguish, we are called to support them rather than flee, as Job's friends do.

sens: son of Othniel and grandson of Kenaz
H2867.detail: Hathath is a man from the tribe of Judah, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the son of Othniel, himself the son of Kenaz and brother of Caleb. His name literally means "one who is afraid" or "timid" in Hebrew, but this does not indicate anything particular about his character. The Bible reports no notable deeds of his.
H2867.origine: The name Hathath comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to tremble" or "to be afraid." This original meaning tells us nothing about the man himself, but simply reflects a common parental naming choice in the Old Testament.
H2867.emploi: Hathath appears only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 4:13, in a genealogy of the tribe of Judah. He is presented there as the son of Othniel, this judge of Israel of whom the Bible recounts elsewhere that he saved the people from the oppression of the Mesopotamians. Hathath is part of those many biblical figures whose name alone remains, without any account of their deeds.

sens: To experience joy, satisfaction
To be content, in a good mood
To rejoice at a happy event
H2868.detail:
1. To experience joy, satisfaction — the feeling of one who is untroubled, who is not threatened. The biblical example shows this clearly: King Darius becomes "very joyful" when he discovers that Daniel has miraculously survived in the lion's den (Daniel 6:23). It is the joy of one who sees danger vanish.

2. To be content, in a good mood — an inner state that is serene and peaceful. This implies an absence of fear and worry. Here, it is the joy of relief: the king realizes that his friend Daniel is alive and unharmed.

3. To rejoice at a happy event — to feel a joy that comes from the heart in response to good news or deliverance. The king moves from worry to complete joy upon witnessing the miracle accomplished.
H2868.origine: The word is the Aramaic peal (simple form of the verb) derived from the root טאב (T-'-B). This root also belongs to the Hebrew יָטַב (yatav, "to be good, to go well"), which expresses the fundamental idea of being in good condition, going well. Aramaic and Hebrew are two closely related languages, cousins, and often share the same roots with very similar meanings. Here, "to be joyful" extends the idea of "going well": when one is doing well, they are naturally joyful.
H2868.emploi: This Aramaic verb appears only once in the Bible: in Daniel 6:23. It describes the emotional reaction of King Darius learning that Daniel has miraculously survived the lion's den. The context shows that this joy arises from an extraordinary event, a wonderful deliverance. The word thus expresses a deep and justified joy, one produced by the manifestation of God's power. Its unique use makes it almost an exceptional word: a moment of royal joy in the face of the miracle.
H2868.portee: This word invites the reader to contemplate how true joy arises from deliverance and trust in God. Seeing the king become "very joyful" upon discovering that Daniel is unharmed after trusting in his God (verse 23) shows us that true joy comes from witnessing God act on behalf of His children. It is a joy that calms fears and celebrates the divine work.

sens: pleasing, suitable
of good quality, pure
H2869.detail:
1. The word designates what pleases the king or the one who judges: in Ezra 5:17, the authorities ask the king to investigate "if the king finds it good," meaning if it is suitable and approved by him. It is a positive value judgment made by someone in authority.
2. It also describes what is of pure or excellent quality: in Daniel 2:32, the head of the statue is made of "pure" gold, meaning gold without mixture, of the best quality. The word then evokes purity and the absence of defect.
H2869.origine: This Aramaic word (טָב) is the Aramaic form of its more common Hebrew equivalent טוֹב (tov), which means "good" and "pleasant." Both derive from a root that primarily evokes what is pleasing to the eye or heart, what is agreeable. The word family includes verbs and nouns expressing goodness, beauty, and quality. This Aramaic term appears mainly in the Aramaic sections of Daniel and Ezra, parts of the Bible written in Aramaic rather than Hebrew.
H2869.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in the Aramaic books. In Ezra 5:17, it expresses royal approval: the local authorities plead with the Persian king to find their request good, meaning to approve it. In Daniel 2:32, it qualifies the purity of the gold that makes up the head of the dream statue. In both cases, the word carries a judgment: either a moral or administrative approval, or an appreciation of material quality.
H2869.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, goodness is never abstract: it consists of being pleasant, appropriate, of good quality. For the believer, seeking what is "good" in the eyes of God means seeking what pleases and suits Him, what is pure and without defect — an invitation to obedience and integrity.

sens: Persian administrative officer in Samaria during the reign of Artaxerxes
H2870A.detail: Thabeel is a Persian government official who serves in Samaria at the time of the return from exile (around the 5th century B.C.). He appears in the official correspondence addressed to King Artaxerxes with other officials to contest the reconstruction work of the temple that the Jews were undertaking in Jerusalem (Ezra 4:7).
H2870A.origine: The name Thabeel comes from Aramaic and means "God is good" (composed of two elements: "good" and "God"). It is a theophoric name, common in the ancient Near East, reflecting the piety or religious convictions of the one who bore it.
H2870A.emploi: Thabeel appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 4:7. He is among the Persian officials and the inhabitants of the region who send a letter to King Artaxerxes to complain about the reconstruction work of the temple in Jerusalem. This mention shows him as a representative of the local Persian authority involved in the political and religious tensions of the return from exile period.

sens: A man proposed as king of Israel during the Syro-Ephraimite coalition war
H2870B.detail: 1. Tabeel is a man whose son was proposed by the kings Pekah (of Israel) and Rezin (of Syria) to become king of Judah in place of King Ahaz. This proposal is part of their conquest plan: they wanted to conquer Judah, take control of it, and place Tabeel's son as a puppet king obeying their orders (Isaiah 7:6). Nothing else is known about this man; he appears only once in the entire Bible, but his name and this plan mark a critical moment in Israel's history.
H2870B.origine: The name Tabeel means "God is good" in Hebrew, composed of two elements: the divine name and the adjective "good." It is a classic theophoric name, characteristic of the ancient Near East. This name reveals nothing particular about the character himself, except that his parents gave him a pious name.
H2870B.emploi: Tabeel is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 7:6. The prophet Isaiah reports the plan of kings Pekah and Rezin to besiege Jerusalem and replace King Ahaz with Tabeel's son. This moment corresponds to the political crisis known as the "Syro-Ephraimite coalition war" (around 735 B.C.). The context shows that Tabeel was probably a man of foreign origin or an opportunist without dynastic legitimacy, a mere political pawn in the game of regional powers.
H2870B.portee: The appearance of Tabeel illustrates how human plans, even those of powerful kings, remain under God's control. This ambitious plan of Pekah and Rezin never came to fruition: God assured the prophet Isaiah that these plans would fail and that Judah would endure. Tabeel's name, quickly forgotten by history, contrasts with the stability of the Davidic line promised by God.

sens: piece of cloth wrapped around the head
head ornament worn by leaders and warriors
mark of dignity and authority
H2871.detail:
1. The turban is a piece of cloth, often colored or precious, wrapped around the head. It is a common Eastern garment among the peoples of the Middle East. In Ezekiel 23:15, the Babylonian and Chaldean leaders wear it with sashes at their waists: it is a distinctive element of their martial elegance.
2. The floating turban, especially when it is brightly colored, signals the wearer as a man of importance: a leader, a warrior, a person of high rank. Worn on the head, it is visible from afar and displays the status of the one who wears it.
3. By its sumptuous appearance and varied colors, the turban expresses the power, wealth, and authority of the one who dons it. It marks the wearer as superior or worthy of respect.
H2871.origine: The Hebrew word טְבוּל (tavul) belongs to the root טבל, which originally means "to dip" or "to plunge." The turban is thus named because the cloth is soaked, dipped in dye to color the threads — hence these bright colors. The turbans of the great Babylonian leaders were renowned for their rare and brilliant dyes, which required this repeated soaking process.
H2871.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 23:15. The prophet describes, in a critical tone, the seduction that the children of Israel felt at the sight of the Chaldean and Babylonian warriors. These men, adorned with colorful turbans and richly decorated sashes, embodied for the Israelite eyes a seductive carnal power — that of distant empires. Ezekiel sees this as a moral threat: the allure of foreign ornaments hides idolatry and unfaithfulness to the Lord.
H2871.portee: This word reveals how Ezekiel denounces the dazzlement of the people of Israel in the face of the appearances of foreign power. The floating turban symbolizes the seduction of carnal empires, which divert the heart from God. For the reader, it is a call not to confuse external splendor with true dignity — that which comes from obedience to God, not from the ornaments of the world.

sens: Elevated part of a place, summit or peak of a mountain
Dominant region or area, territory from which one can see all around
H2872.detail:
1. The word designates the highest part of a region, which dominates the landscape. In Judges 9:37, we see "a people descending from the heights of the land": these are the inhabitants of mountainous or elevated areas who descend towards the plains, like true viewpoints over the entire territory.
2. By extension, it evokes a place of prestige or dominance. In Ezekiel 38:12, "a people... occupying the high places of the land" refers to those who control the high points, strategically important and visible from afar — an image of power and territorial mastery.
H2872.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes something rounded, bulging, or protruding. It shares a kinship with other Hebrew terms designating the belly or something that protrudes. The initial image is very concrete: what stands out, what emerges, what rises naturally — hence the transition to the meaning of height, of a peak.
H2872.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, always to speak of elevated geographical areas. In Judges 9:37, it describes the inhabitants of the heights observing Shechem below. In Ezekiel 38:12, the prophet depicts a people occupying the high lands of the land of Israel, thus showing their dominant and strategic position. The context is each time military or geopolitical: the heights as territorial advantage or observation point.
H2872.portee: This word reminds us that in Scripture, heights are not just geographical: they often symbolize power, control, and dominance. Understanding the concrete meaning of "height" helps to grasp why the prophets speak of these places: it is where power and mastery over a territory are exercised. For the believer, this invites reflection on what it means to "occupy" a place and exercise responsibility or dominance there.

sens: To kill an animal by cutting its throat or neck to prepare it for food
To kill or massacre brutally a person or group
To be put to death violently and mercilessly
H2873.detail:
1. The primary meaning is very concrete: to slaughter an animal, especially livestock (ox, lamb, sheep), for consumption or preparation as a meal. It is an ordinary act of butchery, as when Joseph orders his steward to "kill and prepare" animals to receive his brothers at noon (Genesis 43:16), or when a man steals livestock and slaughters it to sell (Exodus 22:1).
2. The word is also used to describe the brutal massacre of defenseless people. The wicked "slaughter those whose way is upright" (Psalms 37:14), and Jeremiah compares himself to a lamb being led to slaughter, unaware of the evil intentions of his enemies (Jeremiah 11:19). The image remains that of slaughter, but applied to human beings to emphasize the violence and injustice of murder.
3. More generally, the verb expresses the idea of being killed with violence and cruelty, particularly when God announces that the shepherds will be "slaughtered" (Jeremiah 25:34) or that men will be massacred like livestock (Lamentations 2:21).
H2873.origine: The Hebrew verb טָבַח (tavach) comes from a root that expresses the idea of striking, cutting, or slicing. The word is related to a system of Semitic roots associated with cutting and slicing. In the daily life of Israel, it was a common and necessary activity: killing livestock for food. The Bible uses this concrete word to also illustrate the violence of murders, comparing victims to defenseless animals.
H2873.emploi: This verb appears about eleven times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical books and the prophets. It begins with ordinary uses: preparing a meal by slaughtering animals (Genesis 43:16, Exodus 22:1, 1 Samuel 25:11). But gradually, it takes on a dramatic force. The Psalms and the Prophets use it to describe the violence done to the poor and the righteous: the wicked slaughter the innocent (Psalms 37:14), Jeremiah sees himself as a victim led to slaughter (Jeremiah 11:19). Jeremiah and Lamentations finally use it to announce God's judgment: the shepherds and warriors will be slaughtered like livestock (Jeremiah 25:34, Lamentations 2:21). The word thus expresses the evolution of punishment and violent death.
H2873.portee: This word reminds us that God sees the cruelty towards the weak and the innocent. When prophetic texts compare victims to slaughter animals, they denounce injustice: those who cannot defend themselves should not be treated like livestock. Conversely, the announcement that the wicked will be "slaughtered" assures that God does not forget their crimes and that He will finally establish justice.

sens: Action of killing an animal by cutting its throat
Violent death inflicted on many people
Mass destruction or divine judgment
H2874.detail:
1. Slaughtering is primarily the concrete act of killing an animal by cutting its throat, especially for eating or offering as a sacrifice. It is a common act in the lives of shepherds and cooks in the Bible: Joseph orders his steward to go "prepare" an animal (Genesis 43:16). It is a crude and practical term that designates the work of the butcher.
2. The word then extends to the violent and massive killing of people, like a massacre. Ezekiel speaks of a sword "sharpened for slaughtering" the enemies (Ezekiel 21:20), or the prophet describes a great "carnage" in the land of Edom (Isaiah 34:6). The image of the butcher's knife applied to humans underscores the brutal and dehumanizing nature of the killing.
3. Finally, the word takes on a figurative and theological meaning: God's judgment on rebellious peoples. God "destines for the sword" those who have not listened to Him so that they may be "slaughtered" (Isaiah 65:12). It is divine judgment presented under the image of massive and inevitable death.
H2874.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to cut, to slice." It is related to other Hebrew words designating slaughter and butchery. The basic image is that of the blade that cuts: this is why the word applies both to the animal that is killed in the kitchen and to the enemies that are annihilated in war, or to God's judgment that "cuts" through peoples like a priest slaughters a beast.
H2874.emploi: The word appears twelve times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly among the prophets. In concrete passages (Genesis 43:16, Proverbs 9:2), it designates the work of the cook or housewife preparing the meal. But the majority of uses (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel) are prophetic and metaphorical: they describe divine judgment as a massive slaughtering. The prophets use the bloody and crude image of the butcher to show the horror of the punishment awaiting the rebels. No use is abstract or purely metaphorical: the word always retains its link with violent death.
H2874.portee: This word forces the reader to contemplate the raw reality of God's judgment. It is not a smooth and distant theological term, but an image of slaughter that strikes the imagination. For the believer, this reminds us that God's anger towards sin is real and terrible, and that the refusal to listen to the divine word leads to inevitable destruction. But also used for animals offered to God, it shows that even the willing sacrifice is part of the order desired by the Lord.

sens: Son of Nahor and his concubine Reumah
H2875.detail: Thebach is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, at the point where the text lists the descendants of Nahor, Abraham's brother. He is the son that Nahor had with his concubine Reumah, who also bore three other sons: Gaham, Tahasch, and Maaca (Genesis 22:24). Therefore, Thebach belongs to the generation of Isaac's cousins, in the younger branch of Abraham's family.
H2875.origine: The name Thebach means "a slaughter" or "a killing" in Hebrew, from the same root as the word "slaughterhouse." This name evokes the idea of death or destruction, a dark image, but we do not know the real reason for the choice of this name by his parents. Like many names from antiquity, it likely reflects a circumstance or personal desire of the parents at the time of his birth.
H2875.emploi: Thebach is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in Genesis 22:24, in the genealogy of the children that Nahor, Abraham's brother, had with his concubine Reumah. He is among the twelve descendants of Nahor, alongside his three full brothers and eight half-brothers born of Nahor's first wife. This genealogical mention anchors Abraham's family in a broader context and shows that the patriarchal lineage extended well beyond Abraham and his direct descendants.

sens: Soldier or officer responsible for protecting a person or place
Cook attached to the household of a prominent figure
Military chief responsible for executing the king's orders
H2876.detail:
1. The guard is a soldier who protects the king, an officer, or a prison. In Egypt, Potiphar is "chief of the guards" of Pharaoh (Genesis 37:36), meaning he commands the armed men who ensure the security of the palace. Joseph is imprisoned "in the prison, the place of the king's guard" (Genesis 40:3), a militarized building.
2. The guard can also be a cook: he is a trusted man who prepares the master's food. Samuel "said to the cook: Bring the portion that I gave you" (1 Samuel 9:23), showing that this cook executes the orders of the chief.
3. The chief of the guards is the military commander of the king, responsible for carrying out his decisions, including the execution of the condemned and the deportation of captives. Nebuzaradan, "chief of the guards" of the king of Babylon, "took captive those of the people" (2 Kings 25:11), embodying royal authority in person.
H2876.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the action of cooking, transforming by fire. This is why the guard is primarily a cook: he transforms food by cooking. But the king's cook is also his bodyguard, a trusted armed man. The word thus designates one who serves the master, cooks, or protects him, a function very close in ancient royal palaces. In Aramaic (a related language), the same word means "guard" or "officer."
H2876.emploi: This word appears 32 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the story of Joseph in Egypt (Genesis 37-41) and in the accounts of the fall of Jerusalem (2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 39-52). In Egypt, the "guards" are Pharaoh's military servants. During the Babylonian exile, Nebuzaradan, the "chief of the guards," appears as the armed hand of King Nebuchadnezzar, executing the destruction of Jerusalem and the deportation. In 1 Samuel 9, the word refers to a simple cook attached to Samuel. The meaning thus shifts from bodyguard to cook depending on the context.
H2876.portee: This word reminds readers that the security of the king and the well-being of the people depend on trusted men — guards, faithful servants. For Joseph, exiled in Egypt, the existence of guards also represents Pharaoh's absolute power over his subjects. In Jerusalem, the action of the Babylonian chief of guards symbolizes the fulfillment of God's judgment: the Lord allows the pagans to destroy his city, showing that sin has irreversible consequences.

sens: Soldier assigned to protect a king or high-ranking individual
Military charged with executing the sovereign's orders, including death sentences
H2877.detail:
1. A king's guard is an elite soldier, a member of the armed escort that protects the sovereign and watches over his palace. In Daniel 2:14, Arjoc is the chief of these guards, meaning he commands the royal troops.
2. These guards also serve as executors of the king's will: they carry out his orders and apply them, including the most terrible ones. In the same verse, Arjoc "went out to put to death the wise men of Babylon," showing that the royal guards are the instrument of the king's absolute power.
H2877.origine: This Aramaic word comes from a root that means "to kill" or "to slay." Ancient Greek adopted it in the form σπεκουλάτωρ (speculatōr), a term found in accounts of Roman executions. The parent Hebrew word (טַבָּח / tab.bach, number H2876) also designates the executioner or officer who executes the condemned — he is the one who intervenes in ritual sacrifice or the slaughter of livestock.
H2877.emploi: This word appears only once in the Aramaic New Testament in Daniel 2:14, where it refers to Arjoc, chief of the guards of Nebuchadnezzar II, king of Babylon. In this dramatic context, Arjoc receives the order to kill all the wise men of the city — magicians, astrologers, and sages — because they cannot interpret the king's dream. Daniel approaches him and obtains a delay, showing that even the chief of the guards can be influenced by wisdom and diplomacy.
H2877.portee: This account shows that earthly power, even absolute, is never definitive: Arjoc, an instrument of the king's authority, accepts to listen to reason and is persuaded by a young exile. For the believer, this illustrates how the wisdom that God gives can triumph over threats and brutality; it acts not by force, but by intelligence and persuasion.

sens: Meat from an animal slaughtered or killed for consumption
Animal prepared for sacrifice or slaughter
Figuratively: person doomed to death or destruction
H2878.detail:
1. The word literally designates the meat obtained by killing an animal, particularly by slaughtering. In 1 Samuel 25:11, David speaks of the "cattle" he has killed to feed his shearers: this is the fresh meat intended for the meal.

2. It can also refer to the animal itself at the moment it is prepared for sacrifice or slaughter, even before the killing is accomplished. It is this animal that God "takes away" in Jeremiah 12:3, led to its execution.

3. The Bible also uses it figuratively to speak of a person or a people doomed to death. In Psalms 44:23, the believer cries that his people are "regarded as sheep destined for slaughter": an image of those who are defenseless before their persecutors.
H2878.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to strike" or "to slaughter." It describes the brutal action of killing an animal for food. It is found in other Hebrew forms expressing slaughter, sacrifice, or execution, very concrete images in a culture where livestock and animal sacrifice held a central place.
H2878.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. In 1 Samuel 25:11, it simply refers to meat killed to feed David's harvesters. In Psalms 44:23 and Jeremiah 12:3, its usage becomes more dramatic: the slaughtered animal becomes the image of Israel or the persecuted believer, defenseless before a terrible fate. This progression from the concrete to the figurative shows how the Bible transforms a daily reality into a powerful symbol of suffering and abandonment.
H2878.portee: This word reveals how God sees the suffering of his people: not as an absurd injustice, but as something that does not escape him. When the psalmist cries, "we are regarded as sheep destined for slaughter," he does not deny the violence that strikes him, but he addresses it to God who "knows" his heart. It is a call for justice from the God who knows and who can save.

sens: woman who prepares meals
servant in charge of the kitchen in a house or palace
H2879.detail:
1. A cook is a woman who prepares food and meals, in the most direct sense of the term. In 1 Samuel 8:13, Samuel lists what the king will demand from the Israelites: he will take their daughters to make them cooks, meaning women attached to the royal kitchen.
2. The word also designates, more broadly, a servant of a particular rank assigned to the preparation of meals in an important house or palace. It is a role of service, but recognized as a specialized function within the household.
H2879.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to kill" or "to slaughter," hence "one who kills animals for meat." From there, it took on the meaning of "cook," one who prepares meat and meals. It is the feminine form of the word designating the cook or butcher.
H2879.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 8:13. Samuel warns the Israelites of the king's abuses to whom they ask to submit: he will requisition their daughters to make them perfumers, cooks, and bakers. The context shows that it was a personal service, likely at the royal palace, to which the king could call upon to have women with culinary talent at his disposal.
H2879.portee: This passage reminds the believer that asking for a king "like the other nations" exposes the people to losing their freedom and resources. The mention of cooks emphasizes that human power often operates at the expense of the weakest, here the women and young girls. It is an invitation to remain vigilant against the promises of power.

sens: Syrian city conquered by King David
H2880.detail: Thibchath is a Syrian city that belonged to Hadadezer, king of Zobah, a regional power in the northern Levant during David's time. When David defeated Hadadezer, he took the riches of his cities, including Thibchath. The abundant bronze that David found there was later used by Solomon to make the great basin of the house of the Lord, as well as the pillars and utensils of the Temple (1 Chronicles 18:8).
H2880.origine: The name Thibchath means "extension" in Hebrew. The city is also referred to as Betah in the textual tradition. Its name likely reflects its importance or role as a Syrian commercial or military center.
H2880.emploi: Thibchath appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 18:8. It is mentioned as one of the cities that David conquered from King Hadadezer, before the bronze taken from there enriched the Temple project under Solomon. It thus serves as a historical marker of David's reign and his military victories against the Syrian kings.

sens: Briefly immerse an object in a liquid
Slightly wet a part of the body by dipping it in water
Cause a substance to penetrate by soaking it in a liquid
Be soaked or saturated with liquid
H2881.detail:
1. Dip means to plunge something into a liquid, often quickly. When the sons of Aaron dip their finger in the blood (Leviticus 4:6), they immerse it just enough to cover it before using it to sprinkle. It is the action of voluntarily wetting something by placing it in a liquid.

2. The word also describes the moment when a part of the body comes into contact with water: the feet of the priests get wet at the edge of the Jordan (Joshua 3:15). It is the partial and quick immersion of a part of the body in water.

3. Dip can mean soaked or saturated — when someone or something is completely wet by a liquid (Job 9:31: "You would throw me into the mud, and my own skin would abhor me"). The liquid has penetrated completely.

4. The word is also used to express impregnation or mixing: dipping a sponge or cloth in water (Exodus 12:22) means saturating it with water by plunging it.
H2881.origine: The Hebrew verb טָבַל comes from a root that evokes the idea of plunging or immersing. It belongs to a family of words describing contact with liquids. In classical Hebrew, this verb is used in contexts of ritual purification (dipping in water or blood) and preparation of offerings. The root expresses the movement of bringing something into a liquid and taking it out.
H2881.emploi: The verb טָבַל appears 16 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the Pentateuch and historical texts. In Levitical worship, it describes the ritual action of the priests: dipping the finger in blood or oil before sprinkling it on the altar or sanctuary (Leviticus 4:6, 9:9, 14:16). It is also used for purification: dipping the hyssop in water before the purification sprinkling (Numbers 19:18), or bodily immersion (Joshua 3:15; 2 Kings 5:14). The word can also denote complete or symbolic impregnation: the dipping of Joseph's tunic in blood (Genesis 37:31). Its meaning varies little: it is always the action of bringing something into a liquid, briefly or completely.
H2881.portee: This simple, concrete verb reveals how the Bible describes the ritual gestures of purification and worship. To dip is to pass an object or a person through water or blood to prepare, purify, or consecrate them. For the reader, it is a reminder that biblical purification is never abstract: it involves visible gestures, actions of the body. This shows that our relationship with God engages our whole being, including our senses and hands.

sens: Man of the tribe of Levi, doorkeeper of the temple during the divided monarchy
H2882.detail: 1. Thebalia is a Levite from the family of Merarites, son of Hosah. He was one of the doorkeepers of the temple in Jerusalem, responsible for guarding the gates and controlling the entrances — an important service for the religious life of Israel. He is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 26:11 as the third son of Hosah, after Hilkiah and before Zechariah, in the list of doorkeepers organized under King David.
H2882.origine: His name means "purified" in Hebrew, perhaps evoking a consecration or separation for divine service. He belongs to the lineage of the Merarites, one of the three major families of Levites established by Moses for the service of the tabernacle and then the temple.
H2882.emploi: Thebalia appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 26:11. It is in the context of the census that King David conducted of all the Levites to organize the service of the temple. He is presented as one of the many doorkeepers who ensured the guarding of the sanctuary. His brief appearance shows us the importance of hierarchy and organization of worship in the temple, as well as the place of the Levites in this organization.

sens: To penetrate or sink into a material or environment
To be submerged or engulfed in water
To sink into a hole or pit
To be firmly implanted or established
To be plunged into a difficult or dangerous situation
H2883.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to sink something into a material, or to sink oneself into it. The stone thrown by David "sank" into Goliath's forehead (1 Samuel 17:49): it penetrated deeply into his flesh.

2. To sink can mean to be submerged or engulfed in water. The Egyptian fighters were "swallowed" in the Red Sea (Exodus 15:4): the waters completely covered them, and they disappeared.

3. To sink into a hole or pit: the psalmist speaks of nations that "fall" into the pit they have dug (Psalms 9:16), meaning they descend into it to remain imprisoned.

4. To be firmly established or implanted, like the foundations of the earth that are "supported" or solidly sunk (Job 38:6). Here the word describes deep stability.

5. Figuratively, to sink into a difficult or bad situation: the psalmist says "I sink in the mire" (Psalms 69:3) to express that he is plunged into misfortune and without resources.
H2883.origine: The Hebrew verb tabá' expresses the action of sinking or causing to sink. Its root evokes the idea of penetration and depth. The word can have a passive form ("to be sunk") that emphasizes the aspect of being submerged or implanted against one's will. In Hebrew, this root is used to describe both concrete realities (an object sinking, a person sinking in water or mud) and metaphorical situations (sinking into sin or distress).
H2883.emploi: The verb appears about ten times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in poetic and narrative texts. It is particularly found in the Psalms (69:3, 69:15; 9:16), where it describes the distress of the righteous who sinks into the mud and misery, asking God to pull him out of this pit. It also appears in historical accounts (Exodus 15:4; 1 Samuel 17:49) and descriptions of material situations (Jeremiah 38:6; Jeremiah 38:22, where Jeremiah is lowered into a cistern). The context varies: sometimes it involves physical and brutal sinking (the stone in the forehead), sometimes immersion and disappearance (in water), and sometimes gradual sinking or entrapment (in mud, in distress). The word can also describe a firm implantation (Job 38:6).
H2883.portee: This verb helps the reader understand the urgency and depth of the psalmist's distress, who does not just fall but sinks, meaning he can only rely on God to be pulled out. It also expresses divine judgment on those who dig evil: they fall into the pit of their own making (Psalms 9:16). For the believer, this word reminds us that misery is sometimes a sinking from which one cannot extricate oneself alone, and that only divine intervention can "pull out" the one who sinks.

sens: Ancestor of a family of temple servants returned from exile
H2884.detail: Thabbaoth is the name of the founder of a family of Nethinim (temple servants) who accompanied Zerubbabel during the return from exile to Jerusalem. His name means "rings" in Hebrew, likely referring to a long-forgotten object or characteristic. The family is mentioned twice in the records of the exiles who returned: first in Ezra 2:43, where it appears among the listed Nethinim, and then in Nehemiah 7:46 in a parallel list. These two mentions highlight the importance of documenting the genealogies of the temple servants, as they played an essential role in the worship and functioning of the sanctuary.
H2884.origine: The Hebrew name טַבָּעוֹת (tabbaoth) comes from the root טָבַע (tabaa), which means "rings" or "bands." The exact origin of the family nickname remains obscure, but the names of the Nethinim often reflect concrete objects, actions, or particular characteristics. This name fits within the Hebrew tradition of naming family groups after their founding ancestor, thus preserving the lineage through generations.
H2884.emploi: Thabbaoth appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, both times in official lists: in Ezra 2:43 and in Nehemiah 7:46. These two verses are nearly identical and enumerate the families of Nethinim who returned from Babylonian captivity with Zerubbabel in the sixth century B.C. The Nethinim were minor temple servants, distinct from priests and Levites, assigned to practical tasks of worship. The repeated appearance of the name Thabbaoth in these two independent records attests to the historical authenticity of his family and its recognized role in the second temple community.

sens: A small circular object, usually made of metal, worn on the finger or that can be slipped on
Seal ring, a symbol of authority and power used to sign important documents
Metal ring attached to an object for holding, carrying, or securing it
Ornamental ring, jewelry made of gold or precious stone
H2885.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a simple, circular ring typically worn on the finger as an ornament. In Isaiah 3:21, the women of Jerusalem wore rings among their jewelry.
2. The seal ring is an engraved ring used to authenticate acts and official documents: it is an insignia of authority and power. When Pharaoh removes his ring and puts it on Joseph's hand (Genesis 41:42), he confers authority over Egypt to him. Similarly, King Ahasuerus gives his ring to Haman and then to Mordecai to govern in his name (Esther 3:10; 8:2).
3. In the Tabernacle and its objects (the ark, the table, the altar, the grate), gold or bronze rings are fixed at the four corners or sides to pass the carrying bars through. These rings are technical elements, purely functional (Exodus 26:24; 38:5).
4. The ring can also simply be a luxury ornament: Numbers 31:50 mentions the gold rings that the soldiers offered to the Lord, or Exodus 35:22 where the people bring rings among the materials for the Tabernacle.
H2885.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of turning or looping. The ring is the quintessential circular object — a loop closed upon itself. In Greek, the same word σφραγίς (sphragis) often translates the seal-ring of the Old Testament, highlighting the connection between the ring and the act of authenticating and sealing.
H2885.emploi: This word appears 49 times in the Hebrew Bible, predominantly in Exodus and parallel passages that describe the Tabernacle and its sacred objects. The ring is always an architectural or functional element: passing the bars, securing the tents, assembling the pieces of the worship furniture. A few occurrences show the ring as an ornament or symbol of power: Genesis 41:42 (Pharaoh gives Joseph his governing ring), Esther 3:10; 8:2 (rings of kings granting authority), Isaiah 3:21 (jewelry of women). The word never changes its fundamental meaning — it is always a circular object — but its function varies: technical, ornamental, or political.
H2885.portee: For the believer, Pharaoh's ring given to Joseph speaks of delegated power: it is God alone who confers authority, and the one who receives it must manage it faithfully. The rings of the Tabernacle remind us that worship is built according to God's design down to the smallest details: nothing is left to chance. Finally, the ring as a seal evokes signature and authenticity — inviting us to live in accordance with our commitments before God.

sens: Father of the king of Syria Ben-Hadad I
H2886.detail: Thabrimmon is a king of Syria whose name means "Rimmon is good" (Rimmon being a deity worshiped in Syria). He is the father of Ben-Hadad I, a powerful Syrian king who reigns in Damascus during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel. The only biblical account that mentions him is when King Asa of Judah sends messengers to visit him to establish an alliance against Northern Israel (1 Kings 15:18).
H2886.origine: The name Thabrimmon is composed of two elements: "Tav" or "Tob" meaning "good" in Hebrew, and "Rimmon," a Syrian deity. This is a typical theophoric name from the Syro-Aramean world, where the name of the tutelary deity appeared in the person's name. This practice was common among kings and nobles of the Levant.
H2886.emploi: Thabrimmon appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 15:18, where he is identified as the king of Syria based in Damascus and the father of Ben-Hadad I. The context is political and diplomatic: King Asa of Judah sends him a tribute of silver and gold to secure an alliance against the Northern kingdom. This brief mention reveals the political importance of Syrian kings during this period of biblical history, even though Thabrimmon himself plays no direct role in the narrative.

sens: tenth month of the Jewish calendar, corresponding to December-January
H2887.detail: 1. Tebbeth is the tenth month of the Jewish lunar calendar, which roughly corresponds to the period of December-January in our current calendar. It is during this month that Queen Esther was brought to King Ahasuerus for royal service (Esther 2:16).
H2887.origine: The name Tebbeth comes from Hebrew and means "goodness" or "excellence." It designates the tenth month of the ancient Hebrew calendar, which begins in spring with the month of Nisan. This month falls in winter according to our Gregorian calendar, a period characterized by rain and cold in the ancient Near East.
H2887.emploi: Tebbeth appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Esther 2:16, where the author notes precisely the month during which Esther was brought to the royal palace of Ahasuerus. This chronological mention underscores the importance of the event and places the narrative within a sequence of dateable facts. The Jewish calendar remains marked by this same cycle of twelve lunar months.

sens: Place in Canaan mentioned at the time of Gideon's victory over the Midianites
H2888.detail: Tabbath is a geographical site in the region of Canaan where the pursuit of the Midianite armies by Gideon and his three hundred men took place. During the memorable battle reported in Judges 7, after God caused confusion in the enemy camp by making the Midianites turn their swords against one another, they fled. The Bible specifies that their retreat extended "as far as the border of Abel-Meholah near Tabbath" (Judges 7:22), indicating that Tabbath marks a stage or limit in the course of this desperate flight.
H2888.origine: The name Tabbath means "famous" or "renowned" in Hebrew, likely derived from a root evoking fame or notoriety. This name may reflect the historical significance of the site, linked to one of Israel's major military exploits during the time of the Judges.
H2888.emploi: Tabbath appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 7:22. It is mentioned in the context of the retreat of the Midianites after their humiliating defeat at the hands of Gideon. Although not detailed, this geographical reference helps to situate the battlefield and gives a concrete reality to the narrative of this divine miracle where three hundred men routed an innumerable army.

sens: Free from physical or material defilement, especially for a precious substance or food according to the law
Ritually acceptable, conforming to the law, especially for an animal or person in worship
Spiritually and morally innocent, without guilt
Authentic and unmixed, speaking of a precious material
H2889.detail:
1. A substance or food that contains no material impurity. This is the everyday sense: pure gold, without alloy (Exodus 30:3), or the pure gold bells used in the priest's garment (Exodus 39:25). For foods, a pure animal is one that the law permits to be eaten or sacrificed, as opposed to unclean animals (Genesis 7:2: the seven pairs of clean animals that Noah must take into the ark).
2. A person or thing admitted to worship according to divine prescriptions. A bald man can be pure in the sense of the law, even if he has lost his hair (Leviticus 13:40). One who is pure can sprinkle water on one who is unclean to purify him (Numbers 19:19). This is a legal status: it can be obtained through washings and time.
3. Innocent in the spiritual and moral sense, without the stain of guilt. This is the deeper sense: "How can a clean thing come from an unclean?" asks Job (Job 14:4), recognizing that human nature is tainted by sin. The pure in heart shall see God (Matthew 5:8).
4. Unmixed and unaltered, speaking of a precious substance. This is the absolute purity of the material: the pure gold of the worship in the Tabernacle or Temple reflects the holiness of God, which tolerates no imperfection.
H2889.origine: This Hebrew word originally designates what is free from defilement or flaw. It comes from a root that expresses the idea of cleanness and clarity. In biblical Hebrew, purity can be physical (absence of dirt or defect), ritual (conformity to divine prescriptions), or moral (innocence, absence of guilt). It is a central concept in Leviticus, which enumerates clean and unclean animals, foods, and acts according to the Law.
H2889.emploi: This word appears 87 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the books of the Pentateuch (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy) and in Chronicles, where it describes worship in the Tabernacle and Temple. It first applies to materials (pure gold of sacred furniture), animals (clean animals to be sacrificed or eaten), and people (ritual purity obtained through purification). Gradually, it also designates moral and spiritual purity: Job meditates on the impossibility for man to be pure before God (Job 14:4), and the Psalms celebrate the purity of God's words and ordinances (Psalms 12:7, 19:10). The meaning thus expands from ceremonial to moral.
H2889.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that holiness is God's absolute requirement. The law distinguished the clean from the unclean to teach that God accepts only what is without defect. But Job and the Psalms reveal that the true problem is not material or even ritual defilement: it is the sin of the heart. In Christ, those who believe in Him are purified not by washings, but by forgiveness and the transformation of the Spirit, becoming perfectly pure before God.

sens: Free from dirt or filth (in concrete terms)
In accordance with ritual law, without defect (for animals or offerings)
Morally blameless, without guilt
Spiritually separated from evil and sin
H2890.detail: 1. In a concrete and physical sense, "pure" means free from dirt or filth: something clean, without a mixture of foreign material. 2. In the ritual and religious domain, the word designates what is in accordance with God's law, without defect: a pure animal can be offered as a sacrifice, while an impure animal cannot. 3. On a moral and ethical level, "pure" means without guilt, blameless before God: it is innocence or integrity. In Habakkuk 1:13, God's eyes are too pure to see evil — meaning that God, in His absolute holiness, cannot tolerate the presence of sin; His nature is radically separated from evil. 4. The word also evokes spiritual purity: a life, a pure heart is a life devoted to God, without compromise with sin.
H2890.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of shining, clarity, hence "pure" in the sense of clear, unobstructed, without obstruction. The root suggests the absence of dirt that would veil or stain. In the Old Testament, purity is a key concept: it is first ritual (the pure and the impure in Leviticus), then moral (a pure heart, a pure conscience). The word belongs to the vocabulary of divine holiness.
H2890.emploi: The word appears only once in the provided passages, in Habakkuk 1:13, where it characterizes the eyes of God. It is a statement of God's absolute holiness: His vision and nature are so radically pure that they cannot tolerate any trace of evil or iniquity. God cannot and does not want to contemplate evil as something acceptable. This passage establishes a striking contrast: the righteous suffer while the wicked prosper (in verse 13), and yet God, in His purity, cannot ignore this disorder. The affirmation of divine purity is the foundation upon which all appeals to His justice rest.
H2890.portee: This affirmation that God is pure will teach the believer that God can never be complicit in evil, even if He sometimes seems to tolerate injustice. It also reminds that the purity of heart is a central value of faith: to approach the pure God, the believer must seek his own moral and spiritual purity, not by his own strength, but by trusting in the grace of God that purifies.

sens: To be free from physical or ritual impurity, especially from disease or contagion
To perform the purification rites prescribed by the Law
To be morally and spiritually free from guilt and sin
To make pure, to remove what stains
To pronounce someone pure after inspection or rite
To purify oneself, to submit to the purification rites
H2891.detail: 1. The strictly physical sense primarily concerns leprosy and contagious diseases: in Leviticus 13 and 14, we speak of clothing or people who "purify" themselves when the disease is gone, as in Leviticus 13:6 where a sore fades and the person is "pure." 2. Ritual purification is the set of actions prescribed by the Law to become acceptable for worship: washings, sacrifices, waiting periods. Numbers 8:21 describes the Levites who "purify" themselves by washing and presenting an offering. 3. The moral and spiritual sense speaks of the absence of guilt before God: Psalm 51:9 asks God to purify the psalmist's heart, and Proverbs 20:9 wonders who can say, "I have purified my heart." 4. The verb also means "to make pure," that is, to remove the stain: Ezekiel 36:25 promises that God will purify Israel by pouring clean water on them. 5. In the passive form or as an act of the priest, the word designates the act of "pronouncing someone pure" after examination or rite: Leviticus 14:4 speaks of one "who must be purified." 6. Finally, "to purify oneself" can mean consciously preparing to meet God, as Jacob commands in Genesis 35:2 before building an altar at Bethel.
H2891.origine: The Hebrew verb טָהֵר comes from the root טהר which evokes the idea of removing impurities, making clean or bright. The word is close to the Semitic concept of cultic and moral purity. In Aramaic and Arabic, related roots also express cleanliness and clarity. Purity in the Old Testament is both physical (absence of disease or contagion) and spiritual (absence of fault before God), and this verb encompasses both dimensions.
H2891.emploi: This verb appears 79 times in the Old Testament, mainly in Leviticus and Numbers where it describes the legal purification rites. The context is that of Israelite worship: purification after leprosy (Leviticus 13-14), after bodily discharge (Leviticus 15), purification of the Levites before their service (Numbers 8), purification after contact with a dead body (Numbers 19). But the word expands: in 2 Kings 5, Naaman must "purify" himself by bathing in the Jordan to be healed. Among the prophets, the verb becomes metaphorical: Ezekiel speaks of a future moral purification of Israel (Ezekiel 36:25), and Malachi of God who will "purify" the sons of Levi (Malachi 3:3). The Psalms make it a cry of the heart: Psalm 51 implores God to purify the psalmist from his sin.
H2891.portee: The word "purify" shows the Christian reader that God takes impurity—both physical and moral—seriously and offers a path to restoration. The ancient rites of purification are no longer practiced, but they foreshadow the forgiveness and renewal that Christ brings: to be "purified" is to be restored to a right relationship with God. This richness of the term invites the Christian to see that being pure is both the healing of the body and the purification of the heart by grace.

sens: State or quality of what is pure, without stain or mixture
Process or act of cleaning, of making pure what was stained
H2892A.detail: 1. Purification is primarily the state of purity, the quality of what is without blemish or contamination. In Exodus 24:10, when Moses and the elders of Israel see God, the sky under His feet shines "like sapphire, clear as crystal" — it is the image of perfect clarity, without alteration. 2. But the word also designates the process, the act of purifying oneself. A woman who has just given birth, according to Leviticus 12, must "purify herself from her blood" for a certain number of days (33 days for a son, 66 for a daughter). This period of purification is not simply a rest: it is a time defined by the Law during which she prepares to resume her place in the community. Once the days of purification are completed, she brings a sacrifice to the sanctuary (Leviticus 12:6).
H2892A.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root "thr" which fundamentally means "to be pure," "to shine," "to be clean." It expresses the idea of clarity and absence of defect. Purification is the action of making something clear, without stain, ready to be used or presented. The family of this word in Hebrew includes verbs and adjectives related to ritual and spiritual purity, which are very important in the Law of Leviticus.
H2892A.emploi: This word appears four times in the French Bible (2 times translated as "purification," 1 time as "purity," 1 time as "purify"). It is concentrated in the prescriptions of Leviticus (chapter 12) which regulate the purity of women after childbirth. In Exodus 24:10, it characterizes the purity of heaven itself, manifesting divine perfection. In all the uses in Leviticus, purification is never instantaneous: it involves a delay, a waiting period (hence "she will remain thirty-three days to purify herself"), and it culminates with an offering at the sanctuary. It is a serious act, framed by the Law, that brings someone from a state of impurity to one where they can approach the holy.
H2892A.portee: The notion of purification reminds us that in the Bible, sin and impurity create a distance from God. But what the Law establishes is that there is a path, a process to return to purity — not by self-determination, but by obedience to prescriptions given by God. For the Christian under the new covenant, this points to Christ, who alone truly purifies us from our sins and restores us to communion with God.

sens: Bright shine of a brilliant thing
Glory and majesty radiating from someone
H2892B.detail:
1. The word designates the visible shine, the light that a shiny surface or a polished object emits — like the shine of a precious stone or a golden crown. It is the impression of clarity and luster that strikes the eye.
2. Figuratively, it evokes the glory, majesty, and prestige of a person, especially a king: it is the brilliance of his power and honor that impresses. In Psalms 89:45, the psalmist says that God has destroyed the splendor of the king, meaning his royal shine, his visible dignity — his earthly throne is nothing but a ruin.
H2892B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be pure, clear." The starting idea is that of purity and clarity — when a surface is pure and smooth, it shines, it has luster. The meaning then evolves towards visible shine, and then towards moral and social brilliance: the glory of a person or his majesty. It is a rare word in biblical Hebrew.
H2892B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalms 89:45, in a psalm that recounts the humiliation of the king of Israel and the believer's doubt regarding divine promises. The context is that of a king's downfall: it speaks of ending his splendor, that is, all the shine and majesty of his reign. The word describes not only the visible glory of the throne and power but also the honor and dignity that constitute the greatness of a king.
H2892B.portee: This word reminds the reader of the fragility of human power and earthly glory. What shines and impresses — the majesty of a king, the luster of honors — can be shattered by God. This invites the believer not to place his hope in the visible greatness of the world, which does not last.

sens: Action of purifying, cleaning
State of purity achieved
Rite or ceremony of legal purification
Period of purification after a defilement
H2893.detail:
1. The word first designates the action of making pure, cleaning something that is soiled or impure. It is the active process of purification: in Leviticus 14:2, the law describes the conditions of the day when the healed leper begins his purification, that is, his steps to regain a pure state in the eyes of God and the community.
2. The word can also describe the state of purity itself, the result achieved: when a man has been declared pure after examination (Leviticus 13:7, 13:35), it means that the purification is complete.
3. Purification is often a rite or ceremony prescribed by the Law: in Leviticus 14:23, the leper brings his offerings "for his purification" — he fulfills the holy procedure set by God to erase his legal defilement.
4. Finally, the word designates the period itself during which one is in a state of impurity and awaits to be purified: in Leviticus 15:13, the one who has a discharge will count seven days "for his purification," a time of waiting and steps before returning to purity.
H2893.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to be pure, to clean." It evokes the idea of separation and cleanliness: what is pure is separated from defilement. This concept permeates the entire legal system of the Old Testament, where purity is not only hygienic or moral but also and especially spiritual and ceremonial — it allows one to approach God and participate in the religious life of the people.
H2893.emploi: The word appears eleven times in the Old Testament, almost exclusively in Leviticus (laws of legal purity) and in a few historical accounts (Chronicles, Nehemiah, Ezekiel). It is used to designate the rituals of purification after a skin disease (Leviticus 13-14), after a discharge (Leviticus 15), after contact with a dead body (Numbers 6:9), or for the services of the Levites at the temple (1 Chronicles 23:28, Nehemiah 12:45, Ezekiel 44:26). The notion varies according to the context: sometimes it refers to the rite itself, sometimes to the period, sometimes to the examination that determines the pure or impure status. In all cases, it is a regulated and serious process: one must present oneself to the priest, perform specific acts, and wait designated times.
H2893.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that in the Old Testament, purity was a major subject: it marked the separation between what can approach God and what cannot. Although the Mosaic Law ties purity to material gestures and expectations, it points to a deep spiritual reality. For today's Christian, these rites are abolished (see Hebrews 9-10), but the idea remains: only what is purified by Christ can enter into communion with God.

sens: To use a broom to clean or remove something
To annihilate or completely destroy
H2894.detail:
1. To sweep means to use a broom on the floor or a surface to remove dust, debris, or any dirt. It is the concrete action of cleaning that everyone knows. Isaiah 14:23 uses this image: "I will sweep her away with the broom of destruction."
2. Figuratively and more strongly, to sweep means to completely destroy, erase, reduce to nothing. In this passage, God is not just talking about cleaning, but about sweeping Babylon away completely, reducing it to a desolate swamp — it is total and definitive destruction.
H2894.origine: The Hebrew verb ṭe'ṭe' is an intensive form (called Pilpel in Hebrew): it reinforces the idea of the simple verb. This intensive form suggests a repeated, vigorous, or complete action. The basic image is that of a broom sweeping away. The repetition of the root ṭe'-ṭe' creates a continuous movement, like an energetic and relentless sweeping.
H2894.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 14:23. There, God promises to sweep Babylon, the proud city that had exalted itself against Him. Sweeping here is not just a simple cleaning: it is a promise of total and irrevocable judgment, where the destruction will be so complete that the city will be nothing but a desert, an uninhabitable swamp. The image of the broom emphasizes the definitive nature of this ruin.
H2894.portee: This word shows us how God deals with pride and rebellion: He does not merely repress; He radically destroys. But to sweep also means to clean, to purify. For the believer, this word reminds both of the Lord's judgment against sin and His work of purification in the lives of those who obey Him.

sens: To be pleasant to see or experience, to delight the senses
To bring good, advantage, to be beneficial
To be joyful, to rejoice
To be better, to surpass
To please, to receive approval
To act with righteousness, to do what is right
H2895.detail:
1. To be pleasant to see or experience, to delight the senses: this is to recognize something beautiful, pleasing. On the first day of creation, God sees that the light He has just created "was good" (Genesis 1:4) — it is beautiful and satisfies Him. The land where Jacob rests "is pleasant" (Genesis 49:15), meaning it charms with its fertility and beauty.
2. To bring good, advantage, to be beneficial: the word designates what is profitable, what truly helps. If you observe the commandments of the Lord, "you will be happy" (Deuteronomy 19:13) — these acts will bring you good. The psalmist invites: "Taste and see that the Lord is good" (Psalms 34:9), in other words, experience for yourself all the good that God does for you.
3. To be joyful, to rejoice: this is the state of one who tastes happiness. The Israelites murmur: "Who will give us meat to eat? ... the days of Moses in Egypt come to our minds" (Numbers 11:18), for they longed to be "joyful" — to enjoy a pleasant life.
4. To be better, to surpass: the comparison between two things where one prevails over the other. The word expresses superiority or improvement.
5. To please, to receive approval: that which satisfies the judgment of others. King David performs an action that "all the people found good" (2 Samuel 3:36) — it received unanimous assent.
