6. To act with righteousness, to do what is right: to accomplish moral good, to conduct oneself justly. It is to do what is right in the eyes of God.
H2895.origine: This verb comes from the Hebrew root טוב (tov), which fundamentally expresses the idea of what pleases, what is appropriate. The corresponding noun (also טוב, tov) means "good" or "goodness." In Hebrew, it is one of the most common words to describe what is desirable, useful, beautiful, and morally right. The root also appears in proper names and blessings. It is the word used in Genesis when God contemplates His work and declares it good.
H2895.emploi: This verb appears 44 times in the Old Testament, particularly in historical narratives, poetic books, and the prophets. In Genesis, it describes each day of creation that God "sees as good" — it is an aesthetic and ontological judgment. In the historical books, it describes human actions: a decision is "good" (approved), a life is "good" (prosperous). The Psalms use it to sing of the Lord's goodness toward His people: "The Lord is good, for His mercy endures forever" (Psalms 118:1). In prophetic laments, what "is good" in the eyes of the Lord contrasts with human injustice. The meaning thus shifts from the sensory (what pleases the eye) to the moral (what is just) and the spiritual (what comes from God).
H2895.portee: This word invites the believer to recognize God as the source of all good and all beauty. To say that the Lord "is good" (Psalms 34:9) is not an abstraction, but an experience to be lived: to feel and taste His goodness personally. For the disciple, this also means that seeking good, acting justly, and appreciating the beauty of creation is to walk in accordance with the heart of God. Goodness thus becomes a call to imitate God in His works and judgments.

sens: Pleasing to the senses, pleasant to see or taste
Of great value, excellent in its kind
Conforming to what is appropriate, suitable
Morally right, virtuous
Favorable, prosperous, happy
Superior, better (in the comparative)
H2896A.detail:
1. The word "good" primarily designates what pleases the eye or the senses: the trees of the garden of Eden are "beautiful and good for food" (Genesis 2:9), and the girls the king seeks are "beautiful in appearance" (Esther 2:2). It is the impression of pleasure that something makes us feel.

2. It also describes what has great value, what is excellent or rich: in Genesis 2:12, the gold of the land of Havilah is "good," meaning precious and of superior quality. It is to judge the value of a thing.

3. The word applies to what is appropriate, suitable, fitting for the situation: in 1 Kings 8:36, God teaches the "good way" to walk, that which is right and appropriate for the path one should follow.

4. It also expresses moral goodness and integrity: the man of "good" in Proverbs 14:14 is one whose heart is upright. It is the quality of the righteous.

5. It can mean happy, prosperous, favorable: in Genesis 15:15, Abraham "will go to his fathers in peace, in a good old age and rich" — it is the state of one to whom things turn out well.

6. In the comparative, the word becomes "better": when one says that one solution "is better" than another, one is judging and choosing the superior one.
H2896A.origine: The word טוֹב (tov) is a fundamental root of Hebrew that primarily expresses an impression of pleasure and satisfaction. It is a simple adjective that likely originates from a concrete image of warmth, abundance, or completeness. It is found in Aramaic in the form טָב (tav), with the same meaning. The root is extremely ancient and central in Hebrew thought: it runs throughout the Bible, from the first chapter ("God saw that it was good") to the last prayers. It designates both the beautiful, the excellent, the just, and the beneficial — showing how these values are linked in biblical consciousness.
H2896A.emploi: The word "good" appears 359 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, making it very frequent. It is found in all types of texts: the creation narrative (where God judges each day as "good"), the laws ("good way"), the wisdom literature (to describe the righteous man), the history of Israel. In Genesis, it first qualifies the creation itself, then things deemed precious or worthy of desire; kings and servants ask if a land, a woman, a plan is "good." In the laws, it describes just behavior and commandments. The meaning nuances: sometimes very concrete (beautiful, pleasant), sometimes ethical (just), often merging the two — for the Bible, true good must be both beautiful and just.
H2896A.portee: This word reminds us that in the biblical vision, beauty, excellence, and justice are not separate: what is truly good is good for the body, for the soul, and for morality at the same time. When God sees creation and declares it "good," He invites us to recognize that life, matter, legitimate pleasure, and moral order form a whole. For the Christian, this frees from disdain for the body and the world, while reminding that true "good" must always align with what is just and virtuous. It is also an invitation to seek the "good way" — the one that leads to life.

sens: What is good, beautiful, pleasant to see or eat
What brings happiness, prosperity, advantage
What is morally right and good
The totality of goods, wealth, benefits
Happiness, joy, fulfillment
What is favorable, useful, advantageous
H2896B.detail:
1. In the most concrete sense, the word refers to what is good to see or to savor: the trees in the garden of Eden are "good for food" (Genesis 2:9), they attract the eye and satisfy the palate. It is the pleasant, what naturally pleases.
2. It signifies the happiness and prosperity one receives or can enjoy: God "will grant happiness" to the land that yields its fruits (Psalms 85:13), or when an elder like David's friend doubts "knowing what is good" and what is bad, meaning the things that still bring him joy (2 Samuel 19:35).
3. In moral terms, it is what is right and good to do: rejecting evil and "choosing good" (Isaiah 7:15), or "doing good" by acting with kindness and faithfulness (Psalms 14:3 and Proverbs 14:22).
4. The word can refer to the totality of received goods — food, wealth, joy — as a blessing from God: those who seek good enjoy its benefits (Psalms 104:28).
5. It expresses deep and lasting happiness, the satisfaction of living under divine blessing: a man who fears God "will enjoy good" (Psalms 37:3, Ecclesiastes 2:24).
6. More broadly, it refers to what is favorable and advantageous in business, in relationships: doing good to someone, acting for their benefit.
H2896B.origine: The word הטוב (tov) comes from a very ancient root meaning "to be pleasant, agreeable." It is a fundamental word in Hebrew, among the most common. It also appears in other related Semitic languages. In Genesis 1, God looks at His creation and "sees that it is good" — the word is at the heart of theology: the created world is good because God willed it. The family of the word includes verbs and nouns that all express this idea of goodness, beauty, blessing.
H2896B.emploi: The word appears about 89 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the poetic and wisdom books (Psalms, Proverbs, Job, Ecclesiastes) and in Isaiah. Its meaning varies slightly depending on the context. In Genesis and in the laws of Deuteronomy, it refers to what is materially good or what God ordains for the good of the people (Deuteronomy 6:24, 30:15). In Psalms and Proverbs, it expresses the happiness of the righteous who pursue moral good and receive divine blessing (Psalms 23:6, 37:3, Proverbs 14:22). In Job and Ecclesiastes, it nuances the problem of evil and suffering: the righteous may doubt the "good" they receive (Job 2:10, Ecclesiastes 7:14). The word can refer to a physical quality (pleasant), a moral and spiritual benefit (virtue, happiness), or a material blessing.
H2896B.portee: Understanding this word enriches our view of the Christian life. First, it reminds us that the good God wants for us is not purely spiritual: it includes legitimate joy, pleasure, and prosperity. Next, it links moral goodness (doing good, choosing good) to true happiness: a good life is not limited to obeying out of duty; it is a source of deep satisfaction. Finally, it calls us to discern good from evil, not only by the law but through a spiritual maturity that knows how to "reject evil and choose good" — a wisdom that God gives to those who seek Him.

sens: What is good, advantageous, favorable for someone
Prosperity, happiness, material abundance
Benefit, act of kindness received
Kind word, sweet word
Divine favor, blessing from God
Totality of goods, wealth
H2896C.detail:
1. Good primarily refers to what is favorable, advantageous, what suits someone — the opposite of evil or misfortune. It is what makes one well, what leads to prosperity. When David asks the Lord to show him the goodness of the Lord, he is asking to experience His living kindness (Psalms 27:13).
2. Good also refers to material prosperity, abundance: Job dies without having enjoyed any good, meaning without having known comfort and wealth (Job 21:25). It is the state of one who possesses, who has abundance.
3. Good can refer to a concrete benefit, an act of kindness: David says he has done good to Saul, showing him kindness, but Saul has returned evil for good, meaning malice for kindness (1 Samuel 24:17-19).
4. In several passages, good is a word: Jeremiah's brothers speak to him in friendly, sweet words, but with ulterior motives (Jeremiah 12:6). It is the sweetness of the tongue.
5. Good can be the favor, the blessing that God grants: the Lord promises Israel a multitude of good, much good, blessings in abundance (Deuteronomy 28:11; Jeremiah 24:5-6).
6. Collectively, good refers to the totality of possessed goods, the wealth and advantages of a prosperous life.
H2896C.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the same root as the adjective "good" (ṭôv), which is very common in the Bible: "And God saw that it was good" on each day of creation (Genesis 1). The feminine suffix -ah transforms the adjective into an abstract noun, expressing the state or quality: it is therefore the quality of being good, goodness as a lived reality. This family of words (good, well, goodness, well-being) expresses in Hebrew the idea of what is healthy, pleasant, beneficial — the opposite of evil and bad.
H2896C.emploi: The word appears 62 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the wisdom books (Job, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Psalms) and prophetic books (Jeremiah). Its meaning varies according to the context. Very often it signifies material prosperity and well-being: the Lord promises an abundance of good to Israel when it obeys (Deuteronomy 28:11). It also denotes moral goodness, kindness: one "returns evil for good," meaning one responds to a good action with a bad one (1 Samuel 25:21; Proverbs 17:13). Sometimes it simply refers to a sweet word, a kind promise (Jeremiah 12:6). In a few passages, good is what the Lord does for His people, His active blessing (Jeremiah 24:5-6; Jeremiah 32:42). The word can also be plural or collective: "goods" in the sense of wealth (Job 21:25).
H2896C.portee: This word reminds the believer that God is the source of all good — material prosperity, kindness, protection, favor. The Bible does not deny earthly goods; it receives them as a gift from God. But it also warns: returning evil for good is a serious sin (Proverbs 17:13), and coveting good without limit makes the soul bitter (Ecclesiastes 5:10). The Christian must recognize that all good comes from God and respond to divine kindness with gratitude and obedience.

sens: region located east of the Jordan, north or northeast of Gilead
Aramean region of uncertain location
region where mercenaries and fighters gathered
H2897.detail: 1. Tob is a geographical region located east of the Jordan, in the northern or northeastern area of Gilead. It is a distinct territory known to be inhabited or controlled by Arameans. 2. The exact location of this region is uncertain in biblical geography, but it existed as a recognized entity during the time of the judges and the monarchy. 3. Tob was a place of refuge and gathering for fighters: Jephthah fled there when his brothers drove him away, and people without ties gathered around him there (Judges 11:3). Later, the Ammonites recruited mercenaries from there to fight David (2 Samuel 10:6, 10:8).
H2897.origine: The name Tob literally means "good" in Hebrew (from the verb טוב). However, used as a place name, it designates a specific region whose geographical name has been preserved in biblical tradition. The etymology may suggest that this region was fertile or favorable, but the proper name has acquired its meaning as an autonomous location. The region belonged to or was associated with Aramean peoples.
H2897.emploi: Tob appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always in a military or refuge context. In the book of Judges (11:3, 11:5), Jephthah flees to Tob after being rejected by his brothers, and it is from there that the elders of Gilead call him back to fight the Ammonites. In 2 Samuel 10:6 and 10:8, the Ammonites hire fighters from the land of Tob as allies against David. These usages show that Tob was a border territory, accessible for easily recruiting warriors or where a man could find refuge.

sens: Good things, material possessions one has
The fertility and abundance of a land
Beauty, pleasantness, that which pleases the senses
Well-being, happiness, prosperity
Moral excellence, benevolent generosity
God's goodness toward His people
H2898.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to concrete goods, valuable possessions: Abraham's servant takes his master's "goods" (Genesis 24:10), and later Joseph offers his Egyptian brothers the "best produce" of the land (Jeremiah 2:7). It is what one possesses and what has value.
2. It also evokes the fertility of the soil and its fruits: God promises a land "full of all kinds of good things" (Deuteronomy 6:11), providing food abundantly. This conveys the idea of natural wealth and generous yield.
3. The word can denote beauty and pleasantness: that which delights the heart and senses, creating an atmosphere of joy. This is why God offers His people a land of delights and enjoyment.
4. It expresses the happiness and prosperity one experiences: living in well-being, enjoying the fruits of one's labor or divine grace (Psalms 128:5). The idea is one of a good and happy life.
5. In a moral sense, it becomes excellence, generosity, active benevolence: the quality of one who acts in favor of others. Psalm 145:7 speaks of the "great goodness" of the Lord, which is His creative mercy toward all.
6. Specifically, it is God's goodness: His faithful and benevolent love toward His people (Psalms 27:13). The psalmist desires to see this goodness in action in the land of the living.
H2898.origine: The word tuv comes from a root that expresses the idea of what is good, appropriate, fitting. In Hebrew, the family of the word includes terms denoting good, beauty, and goodness. The word is ancient and fundamental: it appears as early as the first chapter of the Bible ("God saw that it was good"). It is a universal word in Semitic languages to express what satisfies, benefits, and is beautiful and good.
H2898.emploi: The word tuv appears 31 times in the Old Testament. It is found everywhere: in historical narratives (Genesis, Exodus), laws (Deuteronomy), poetry (Psalms, Proverbs), and the prophets. Its meaning varies according to context: material when it speaks of wealth and harvests, moral when it denotes virtue, spiritual when it evokes God's goodness. The usages show that "goodness" can be what one receives from God (His blessings), what one possesses (our goods), and what one recognizes in God (His benevolent nature). It is a key word to express all that is good and comes from God.
H2898.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that all good—our possessions, our food, our joy—comes from God's goodness. Recognizing divine goodness is to learn gratitude and obedience. The word also invites us to cultivate this goodness toward others: since God has filled us with good things, we are called to share the flavor of it with those around us. It is a word that unites material blessing and spiritual transformation.

sens: A Levite sent by King Jehoshaphat
H2899.detail: Tobadonijah is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when King Jehoshaphat of Judah undertakes a religious reform by sending teachers throughout the cities of the kingdom to instruct the people in the Law of God (2 Chronicles 17:8). He is listed among the five Levites and two priests chosen for this teaching mission.
H2899.origine: His Hebrew name literally means "my Lord is good" ("tob" = good, "Adonijah" = my Lord). It is a theophoric name, common among the Hebrews, expressing trust in God's goodness. The same element "Adonijah" appears in other biblical names, such as that of David's son.
H2899.emploi: Tobadonijah is mentioned only once in Scripture, in 2 Chronicles 17:8. He belongs to the period of the divided monarchy, during the reign of Jehoshaphat in the 9th century BCE. His inclusion in the list of teachers reveals the importance the king placed on the transmission of the Torah and the religious instruction of the people, even in small towns.
